Vignette: Arjun

Arjun is a 35-year-old South Asian man who works as a tax consultant at a mid-sized accounting firm in the city. He is married to his wife of six years, Priya, and by most outward measures his life looks orderly and contained — spreadsheets, client calls, dinner at seven. But there is a version of Arjun that existed before the numbers, and that version has followed him home in ways he cannot fully explain to anyone, including himself.

In his late twenties, before he transitioned into finance, Arjun spent fourteen months volunteering with a humanitarian relief organization deployed to a conflict zone in the Middle East. He had gone with idealism and a background in logistics, believing he could contribute something meaningful. For a while, he did. He coordinated supply chains, managed distribution of food and medical aid, and worked alongside local staff who became, in his words, "the most resilient people I have ever known." Then, during his eleventh month, a convoy he had helped organize was struck. Two local colleagues were killed. A third lost his leg. Arjun was not in the vehicle — he had stayed behind that morning due to a minor illness — and that fact, the sheer randomness of it, has never stopped feeling like an accusation.

He returned home within weeks and, wanting to move forward, enrolled in a postgraduate accounting program. He told himself the transition made sense. He needed stability. He needed something he could control. He married Priya two years later and built the quiet, professional life he had imagined. For a time, the strategy seemed to work.

But the past does not stay filed away. Arjun finds that certain things — the sound of a car backfiring, footage of conflict on the evening news, even the particular quality of late-afternoon light in summer — pull him back with a force that feels physical. He is suddenly not in his office or his kitchen but on a dusty road, replaying the morning he stayed behind, convinced that if he reconstructs the sequence of decisions carefully enough, he will eventually find where he went wrong. He never does.

At work, Arjun is meticulous to the point of rigidity. His colleagues regard him as exceptionally thorough, though some find him difficult to read. What they do not see is that the precision is partly a way of staying anchored — if every figure is accounted for, if every column balances, the ground beneath him feels less likely to give way. Still, concentration deserts him without warning. He will be mid-way through a tax return and realize he has read the same line four times, his mind elsewhere entirely.

Nights are the hardest. He sleeps lightly and badly, waking in the early hours with his heart already pounding, the details of the dream dissolving before he can catch them but the dread remaining, thick and certain. He gets up rather than lie there. Priya has stopped asking why, which he tells himself is a relief and suspects is something else.

He has become careful about what he allows himself to feel. Anger surfaces sometimes, sharp and disproportionate — at a slow driver, at a misplaced file — and he is ashamed of it afterward. More often there is a flatness, a sense of watching his own life from a slight remove, as though the warmth he knows he should feel toward Priya, toward the small pleasures of their shared life, is passing through glass before it reaches him. He loves her. He is certain of that. But certainty and feeling are not always the same thing, and the distance between them is one he does not know how to close.

He has not spoken to anyone about the convoy. Not in full. He carries the names of his two colleagues — Tariq and Yusuf — the way a person carries something fragile, always aware of the weight, never quite sure where to set it down.
